title: The hypertrophy series: pairing neurological adaptation and muscle gains
summary: NH explains neurological adaptation, which he calls technical points. It is the learned ability to perform and recruit muscles in a lift, and it caps out after weeks to months. After that, strength gains reflect muscle (or mass) gains. Technique also regresses without practice, so keep each pattern trained at least weekly, using frequency and close variations rather than volume.
claims: Neurological adaptation (technical points) is the body's learned ability to perform a movement pattern
Babies squat ass-to-grass perfectly by instinct; we unlearn it with age but can always recover it
He considers real training to begin once you have learned the technical ability to perform the big lifts
Technical mastery takes weeks to months depending on the lift's technical rating and ceiling: a curl maybe two weeks, a snatch maybe a year
Untrained people recruit muscle poorly, so the weight they move does not reflect their actual strength
Everyone can eventually max out the neurological side; there is a technical ceiling, and after that strength comes from muscle or mass gain
Novices adding 10 lb a week are mostly gaining neurological adaptation, not muscle
The claim that all strength gains could be neurological is wrong and demoralizing; after a month to a year your technique has peaked, and further strength gains are muscle
Unless you drastically change technique or stance, past that point any pound added to the bar is muscle gain
Presses, overhead press especially, regress fast when not practiced, probably because of the small muscles involved
Squat and deadlift technique regresses slowly; a week off often costs nothing
Time spent not training a lift lets technique regress, and it takes as long to regain
Technique gains and losses come fast, while muscle gains and losses come slowly; after long breaks the body looks similar even though its function has changed
Close variations, like paused squats for the back squat, maintain technical points for the main lift
Programs where a movement pattern goes unpracticed for a full month are catastrophic for bodybuilders
Make sure every pattern comes back at least once a week
If you bench only once a week, move some of that volume to a second horizontal press on another day to maintain technique
Technical mastery depends on frequency, not volume, which is why claims that frequency does not matter are wrong
Three hours of squats in one session gives about 45 minutes of technical stimulus; one hour three times a week triples it
There is no point breaking the technical ceiling, but there is in keeping technique at its highest level
